facts.title: Densest natural element
facts.text: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, with a measured density of about 22.59 grams per cubic centimetre. That means a litre of osmium would weigh more than 22 kilograms, roughly twice the density of lead. It edges out its neighbour iridium for the top spot, and the difference is so small that careful X-ray crystallography was needed to settle the contest.

facts.title: Named for its smell
facts.text: The English chemist Smithson Tennant discovered osmium in 1803 in the dark residue left when crude platinum was dissolved in aqua regia. He named it from the Greek word 'osme', meaning smell or odour, because its oxide gives off a sharp, irritating aroma. That oxide, osmium tetroxide, is the source of the pungent scent that betrayed the new metal.

facts.title: A genuinely toxic vapour
facts.text: Osmium tetroxide (OsO4) is volatile even at room temperature and is highly poisonous, attacking the eyes, skin, and lungs in tiny concentrations. It can cause corneal damage and a temporary blindness sometimes called 'osmium poisoning'. Because of this hazard, the pure metal is usually kept in massive form, since powdered osmium slowly reacts with air to form the dangerous oxide.

facts.title: Hard to melt, hard to work
facts.text: Osmium has one of the highest melting points of all metals, around 3033 degrees Celsius, and it is extremely hard and brittle. This combination makes it very difficult to machine or cast, so it is rarely used as a pure metal. Engineers instead exploit its hardness by alloying it with other platinum-group metals.

facts.title: Tips that never wore out
facts.text: For decades osmium found a niche in long-lasting hard tips for instruments that take heavy mechanical punishment. Alloyed with iridium, it formed the durable points of premium fountain-pen nibs, phonograph styluses, and compass and instrument pivots. A pen tipped with 'osmiridium' could write for years without the point grinding away.

facts.title: A staining trick for biologists
facts.text: In laboratories osmium tetroxide is prized as a fixative and stain for electron microscopy. It binds to the fatty lipids in cell membranes and deposits heavy osmium atoms there, making those structures stand out sharply under the electron beam. This single chemical quirk has helped reveal the fine architecture of cells, from membranes to nerve fibres.

facts.title: The rarest of the eight
facts.text: Osmium is one of the scarcest stable elements in Earth's crust, with an abundance of roughly 0.001 parts per million. It belongs to the six platinum-group metals and is recovered mainly as a by-product of refining nickel and platinum ores, especially from deposits in South Africa and Russia. Only a few tonnes are produced worldwide each year.

facts.title: A clock inside the rocks
facts.text: Two of osmium's isotopes power a precise geological dating method. Rhenium-187 slowly decays into osmium-187 over billions of years, so measuring the rhenium-osmium ratio lets geochemists date ores, oil source rocks, and meteorites. The same system helps scientists trace how Earth's core and mantle separated early in the planet's history.

facts.title: Forged in exploding stars
facts.text: Like other heavy metals, osmium was not made on Earth but in violent cosmic events. Its atoms were built up by rapid neutron capture, the so-called r-process, in supernova explosions and in the collisions of neutron stars. The osmium in a museum sample is therefore older than the Sun, scattered through space before our solar system formed.

facts.title: Stretching the periodic record
facts.text: Osmium holds another superlative: among the elements it has one of the lowest compressibilities, resisting being squeezed even under enormous pressure. In high-pressure experiments osmium has stayed stubbornly rigid past 750 gigapascals, far beyond the pressure at the centre of the Earth. This near-incompressibility makes it a favourite test material for studying matter under extreme conditions.
